name: Suloev Stretch
summary: The Suloev Stretch is a knee-compression submission from top half guard and leg-control positions in which the attacker folds the opponent's lower leg and drives the heel toward their buttock, crushing the calf into the hamstring while loading the knee joint.
description: Master the Suloev Stretch in BJJ. Devastating knee compression submission from top half guard and leg control positions. Complete attacker and defender guide.
overview: Named after Russian MMA fighter Amar Suloev, this technique earned its reputation in no-gi and MMA competition, where folding an opponent's leg against itself produces rapid, fight-ending taps even against seasoned grapplers. The position is typically entered from top positions where the attacker has isolated one of the opponent's legs — most commonly half guard top, knee shield passing sequences, or leg entanglement transitions. Unlike straight ankle locks that attack the ankle or kneebars that hyperextend the joint, the Suloev Stretch creates a bending compression: the practitioner's body weight drives the opponent's heel toward their own buttock while the calf is crushed against the hamstring, layering knee-joint stress on top of severe muscular compression. The finishing pressure comes from hip extension and precise angle creation rather than raw pulling force, so positional control through the entry and the finish is what separates a clean tap from a scramble. Because the structures under attack are dense and unforgiving, understanding the biomechanics of knee compression and maintaining unhurried, progressive pressure are essential for both safe training and reliable competition application.

injury_risks.injury: Posterior knee ligament damage (PCL tear or strain)
Calf muscle tear or severe strain

safety_considerations.application_speed: EXTREMELY SLOW - 5-7 seconds minimum in training, progressive pressure only
tap_signals: Multiple rapid hand taps on opponent or mat
release_protocol: Immediately stop all forward hip pressure and extension
Release the leg from the figure-four configuration
Allow the leg to extend naturally without forcing
Create space by moving your hips backward
Check partner's condition before continuing training
training_restrictions: Never apply competition speed or explosive pressure in training
Never spike or jerk the submission - smooth progressive pressure only
Never continue pressure after partner taps
Never practice on partners with existing knee injuries without explicit permission
Always communicate during slow practice to calibrate pressure
Always allow clear tap access for training partner

variations_and_setups.variation_name: Suloev Stretch from Half Guard Top
variations_and_setups.description: The most common entry point, where you have top half guard and your opponent is using a knee shield or defending. As you address their knee shield and start to pass, you can catch their leg in the figure-four configuration and finish the submission before completing the pass.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent is defending half guard with bent leg postures, especially when they refuse to extend the leg for traditional passing

variations_and_setups.variation_name: Suloev Stretch from Knee Shield Pass
variations_and_setups.description: When passing the knee shield position, instead of fully clearing the leg, you can step over and establish the figure-four lock while their leg is still partially in front of you. This allows you to finish the submission mid-pass, catching them before they can recover guard.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent has strong knee shield frames and you feel their leg beginning to extend or create space during your passing attempt

variations_and_setups.description: When opponent turtles and you have control from the top, you can hook one of their legs with your feet, establish the figure-four lock, and finish the submission while maintaining chest pressure on their back. This variation requires good balance and often involves rolling them to their side as you secure the lock.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When attacking turtle position and opponent keeps their legs defensive or folded underneath them, presenting the opportunity for leg entanglement

variations_and_setups.variation_name: Modified Suloev Stretch with Twisting Pressure
variations_and_setups.description: An advanced variation where you add rotational torque to the compression by adjusting your hip angle and creating a slight twisting motion on the knee joint. This combines the compression with rotational stress, increasing effectiveness but also increasing injury risk.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Against extremely flexible opponents where standard compression alone may not be sufficient, or in competition situations where standard application is being defended (use with extreme caution in training)

attacker.name: Suloev Stretch Attacker
attacker.description: Finish the Suloev Stretch: figure-four the trapped leg, drive the heel to the buttocks, and apply slow hip extension to compress the knee and calf for the tap.
attacker.overview: As the attacker you are converting leg control into a finishing knee compression, and the entire submission lives or dies on the quality of your figure-four and the angle of your hips. Your job is to trap the opponent's lower leg so their heel is pinned against their own backside, then use bodyweight and hip extension — not arm strength — to fold the calf into the hamstring and load the knee joint. Because the finishing structures are dense and the tap arrives suddenly, you must win the positional battle first: kill their ability to straighten the leg or rotate their hip away, and only then apply pressure. Rushing the finish before the leg is isolated lets the opponent kick free and reverse the entanglement; patient, layered control followed by slow extension is what produces the consistent tap.
key_principles: Isolate the leg before you compress — the heel must be trapped against the opponent's own buttock with no path to straighten the knee before you apply any finishing pressure.
Generate the finish from hip extension and bodyweight, never from pulling with the arms; the arms only maintain the figure-four while your hips drive the compression.
Control the opponent's hip and far side so they cannot rotate away or invert to relieve the angle — a mobile hip defeats the submission.
Keep the knee line and the compression vector aligned; the heel should travel toward the buttock and slightly toward the centerline to stack calf against hamstring.
Stay chest-heavy and connected so the opponent cannot create the space needed to kick the leg free or scramble to a counter-entanglement.
Apply pressure progressively and read the tap early — the dense knee and calf structures fail fast, so smooth incremental loading replaces any explosive motion.
setup_requirements: Top control over one of the opponent's legs, typically from half guard top, a stalled knee-shield pass, or a turtle leg-ride.
A secured figure-four (or equivalent ankle/foot trap) folding the opponent's lower leg so the heel points toward their own buttock.
Control of the opponent's hip on the attacking side to prevent them rotating away from the compression.
Your bodyweight stacked over the trapped leg so hip extension translates directly into compression rather than the opponent absorbing it as slack.
Awareness of the opponent's far-side framing and free leg so you can shut down the kick-out and reversal before finishing.

execution_steps.description: From top half guard or a stalled pass, pin and isolate the opponent's near leg, clearing their framing so their lower leg is exposed and you can begin folding it.

execution_steps.action: Fold the lower leg and trap the foot
execution_steps.description: Bend the opponent's knee and bring their heel toward their own buttock, trapping the foot with a figure-four of your legs or by clamping the instep against your hip so the knee cannot straighten.
Pin or hook the opponent's hip on the attacking side so they cannot rotate away or invert; without hip mobility the opponent loses the primary escape and the compression angle stays intact.

execution_steps.action: Stack your weight over the trapped leg
execution_steps.description: Drop your chest and shift your bodyweight directly over the folded leg so that any hip extension you produce loads straight into the calf and knee rather than feeding slack into the entanglement.

execution_steps.action: Drive the heel toward the buttock
execution_steps.description: Using your hips and bodyweight, press the trapped heel down and toward the opponent's backside, beginning to crush the calf muscle into the hamstring while the bent knee absorbs the compressive load.
Slowly extend your hips and lever the compression on, increasing the fold of the knee and the calf-to-hamstring crush in a smooth progressive motion until the opponent taps.
Watch for verbal or physical taps and any sudden pain reaction; the moment a tap registers, immediately stop hip extension and let the leg straighten naturally without forcing.

common_counters.counter: Opponent straightens the trapped leg before the figure-four is locked
common_counters.your_response: Re-fold the knee immediately and clamp the instep; if the leg is fully extended, switch to a kneebar or ankle attack rather than forcing a failed compression.

common_counters.counter: Opponent rotates their hip away from the compression to unload the angle
common_counters.your_response: Pin the hip and follow the rotation with your chest, re-stacking your weight so the heel-to-buttock vector is restored before re-applying pressure.

common_counters.counter: Opponent kicks the free leg through and reverses into a counter-entanglement
common_counters.your_response: Maintain inside position and hand-fight for your own leg control; if you are losing the entanglement, retreat to top half guard rather than chasing the lost leg.

common_counters.counter: Opponent grips your near leg and bridges to create scrambling space
common_counters.your_response: Re-establish chest pressure and re-pin the hip, killing the bridge before it generates the space needed to free the trapped leg.

common_errors.error: Applying compression before the leg is fully isolated
common_errors.consequence: The opponent straightens the knee and kicks free, often reversing into a dominant leg entanglement
common_errors.correction: Confirm the heel is trapped against the buttock and the knee cannot straighten before adding any finishing pressure

common_errors.error: Pulling with the arms instead of driving with the hips
common_errors.consequence: The finish stalls and your arms fatigue while the opponent works their escape
common_errors.correction: Use the figure-four only to maintain the trap and generate all compression from hip extension and bodyweight

common_errors.error: Letting the opponent's hip stay mobile
common_errors.consequence: The opponent rotates away, unloads the compression angle, and recovers the leg or scrambles to a counter
common_errors.correction: Pin or hook the attacking-side hip and follow any rotation with your chest before re-applying pressure

common_errors.error: Floating your weight off the trapped leg
common_errors.consequence: Hip extension feeds slack into the entanglement rather than compression, and the submission produces no finishing pressure
common_errors.correction: Stay chest-heavy and stacked directly over the folded leg so every degree of hip extension loads the knee and calf

common_errors.error: Cranking explosively for a fast tap
common_errors.consequence: Dense knee and calf structures can be injured before the opponent can physically tap, creating serious training and competition risk
common_errors.correction: Apply slow, progressive pressure and read the tap early; the compression finishes reliably without any sudden or jerking motion

common_errors.error: Ignoring the opponent's free leg and far-side frames
common_errors.consequence: The opponent bridges or frames into space, kicks the free leg through, and reverses the position
common_errors.correction: Monitor and control the free leg and far-side frames so the opponent cannot generate the space needed to escape

training_progressions.description: With a compliant partner, drill entering from top half guard and folding the lower leg into the figure-four trap, confirming the heel is pinned to the buttock without applying compression.

training_progressions.focus: Killing the hip and stacking weight
training_progressions.description: Add the hip pin and weight stack against light resistance, focusing on preventing your partner from rotating away or straightening the leg while you maintain the trap.
Introduce extremely slow finishing pressure with constant communication, learning to feel the compression threshold and releasing immediately on the tap to keep the drill safe.
From positional sparring in half guard top and leg-ride situations, hunt the entry against full resistance while keeping all finishes controlled and progressive.
Drill flowing between the Suloev Stretch and kneebars, ankle locks, and heel hooks when the primary attack is defended, building a connected leg-attack system for live rounds.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the Suloev Stretch attack?
flashcards.answer: It attacks the knee joint and the calf muscle simultaneously — the bent knee is loaded under compression while the calf is crushed against the hamstring as the heel is driven toward the buttock.

flashcards.question: What must be true about the trapped leg before you apply any finishing pressure?
flashcards.answer: The opponent's heel must be folded and trapped against their own buttock with the knee unable to straighten; if the leg can extend, the compression has no structure to work against and the opponent will kick free.

flashcards.question: Your opponent rotates their hip away from the compression — what does this tell you and how do you respond?
flashcards.answer: Hip rotation is the primary escape because it unloads the compression angle; you must pin the hip and follow the rotation with your chest to restore the heel-to-buttock vector before re-applying pressure, otherwise the opponent recovers the leg.

flashcards.question: Where should the finishing power of the Suloev Stretch come from?
flashcards.answer: From hip extension and stacked bodyweight, not from pulling with the arms; the figure-four only maintains the trap while your hips drive the heel down and toward the buttock to compress the calf and knee.

flashcards.question: Your opponent posts and tries to bridge to create space — what adjustment prevents the escape?
flashcards.answer: Re-establish chest pressure and re-pin the attacking-side hip to kill the bridge before it generates space; staying chest-heavy and connected removes the room the opponent needs to free the trapped leg or scramble.

flashcards.question: Why does floating your weight off the trapped leg cause the submission to fail?
flashcards.answer: Floating your weight lets hip extension feed slack into the entanglement instead of compression, so no finishing pressure reaches the knee or calf; you must stay stacked directly over the folded leg for the finish to load.

flashcards.question: Why must the Suloev Stretch be applied slowly and progressively in training?
flashcards.answer: The knee and calf are dense, unforgiving structures that can be injured before a partner can physically tap; slow progressive pressure with clear communication lets the partner tap safely and prevents PCL, meniscus, and calf injuries.

flashcards.question: What signs indicate the compression is reaching its breaking point and you should be ready to release?
flashcards.answer: A sudden increase in resistance giving way, the opponent's verbal distress or rapid tapping, and a sharp pain reaction; because the tap comes fast, you should expect it and be prepared to release hip extension instantly.

flashcards.question: In competition, how do you keep the Suloev Stretch high-percentage when opponents defend the entry?
flashcards.answer: Use it as part of a connected leg-attack chain — when the compression is defended, immediately flow to a kneebar, ankle lock, or heel hook from the same control, forcing the opponent to defend multiple threats rather than one.

flashcards.question: If the opponent fully straightens the trapped leg before you lock the finish, what is the better option than forcing the compression?
flashcards.answer: Switch attacks rather than forcing a failed compression — a straightened leg is exposed to a kneebar or straight ankle lock, so transition to those finishes instead of fighting to re-fold against a strong defense.

defender.name: Suloev Stretch Defender
defender.description: Defend the Suloev Stretch: recognize the leg fold early, straighten the knee and rotate your hip out before the heel is trapped against your buttock, and escape to safety.
defender.overview: As the defender your safety depends almost entirely on early recognition, because the Suloev Stretch attacks dense knee and calf structures that give very little warning before the tap. The danger begins the moment the attacker folds your lower leg and starts driving your heel toward your own buttock; once that fold is locked and your hip is pinned, escape becomes extremely difficult and forcing it risks serious injury. Your priorities are to feel the leg being folded before it is trapped, to fight to keep the knee straight and the hip mobile, and to rotate away from the compression to unload the angle. If you cannot prevent the trap, recover the position by kicking the free leg through to reverse the entanglement or by clearing the trapped foot before the attacker stacks their weight. Above all, tap early to compression on the knee or calf rather than testing your tolerance against a structure that fails suddenly.
key_principles: Recognize the attack early — the fold of your lower leg and the heel travelling toward your buttock are the first and most important warning signs.
Fight to keep the knee straight; a leg that cannot be folded cannot be compressed, so resist the bend before the figure-four is locked.
Keep your hip mobile and rotate away from the compression to unload the finishing angle before the attacker stacks their weight.
Hand-fight to clear the trapped foot and prevent the attacker from securing the figure-four that locks the heel against your buttock.
Use your free leg actively — kicking it through or framing with it lets you reverse the entanglement or create the space to escape.
Tap early and verbally to knee or calf compression; the structures under attack fail fast and are not worth testing for the sake of a position.
recognition_cues: Your lower leg is being folded and your heel is being driven toward your own buttock.
The attacker stacks their chest and bodyweight directly over your bent leg, pinning your hip on that side.
A building compressive ache in the calf and a pinching pressure behind the knee as the figure-four tightens.
Loss of your ability to straighten the trapped knee or rotate your hip away from the attacker.

defensive_options.action: Straighten the trapped leg before the fold is locked
defensive_options.when_to_use: At the first sign the attacker is folding your lower leg, before the figure-four is secured
defensive_options.if_successful: You deny the compression structure and the attacker stays in top half guard without the submission
defensive_options.risk: Committing to extension can expose the leg to a kneebar if the attacker switches attacks

defensive_options.action: Rotate your hip away from the compression
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the leg is trapped but the attacker has not yet stacked their full weight and killed your hip
defensive_options.if_successful: The compression angle unloads and you can begin clearing the trapped foot
defensive_options.risk: Rotating into the attacker rather than away can deepen the entanglement

defensive_options.action: Kick the free leg through to reverse the entanglement
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the trap is set but you still have an active free leg and framing space
defensive_options.if_successful: You reverse into your own top control or a counter leg entanglement, escaping the compression
defensive_options.risk: A mistimed kick can give up your back or feed a deeper leg attack

defensive_options.when_to_use: When the heel is locked to your buttock, your hip is pinned, and the compression is increasing with no escape available
defensive_options.risk: Delaying the tap risks PCL, meniscus, or calf injury that can take months to heal

escape_paths: Extend the knee and recover top half guard before the figure-four locks
Rotate the hip out and clear the trapped foot to re-pummel the legs
Kick the free leg through to reverse into a counter leg entanglement

favorable_outcomes.how: By straightening the knee and rotating the hip out early, you deny the compression and leave the attacker stalled in top half guard with no submission.
By kicking the free leg through while you still have framing space, you reverse the entanglement and come up into your own bottom-to-top scramble.

common_errors.error: Recognizing the attack too late, after the heel is already trapped against the buttock
common_errors.consequence: The compression structure is locked and escape becomes extremely difficult and dangerous
common_errors.correction: Train early recognition so you feel the leg being folded and react before the figure-four is secured

common_errors.error: Allowing the knee to bend instead of fighting to keep it straight
common_errors.consequence: The bent knee gives the attacker the fold they need to compress the calf and load the joint
common_errors.correction: Resist the bend actively and keep the leg long until you can clear the foot or rotate away

common_errors.error: Staying flat and letting the hip get pinned
common_errors.consequence: A pinned hip removes your primary escape and locks the compression angle in the attacker's favor
common_errors.correction: Keep the hip mobile and rotate away from the compression before the attacker stacks their weight

common_errors.error: Testing your tolerance instead of tapping to compression
common_errors.consequence: The knee and calf fail suddenly, turning a lost position into a serious injury
common_errors.correction: Tap early and verbally to knee or calf compression; the position is never worth a months-long injury

flashcards.question: What is the earliest and most important warning sign that you are being attacked with a Suloev Stretch?
flashcards.answer: The fold of your lower leg with your heel being driven toward your own buttock; recognizing this before the figure-four locks is your best chance to straighten the leg and escape safely.

flashcards.question: Why is keeping your knee straight the key to defending the Suloev Stretch?
flashcards.answer: A leg that cannot be folded cannot be compressed; if you keep the knee straight you deny the attacker the bent-knee structure they need to crush the calf and load the joint, stalling the attack.

flashcards.question: When should you tap to the Suloev Stretch rather than continue defending?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately once the heel is locked to your buttock, your hip is pinned, and the compression is building with no escape; the knee and calf fail suddenly, so testing your tolerance risks a months-long injury.

flashcards.question: How does rotating your hip help you escape the compression?
flashcards.answer: Rotating the hip away from the attacker unloads the finishing angle that drives the heel into your buttock, relieving the compression and creating the space needed to clear the trapped foot and recover position.

flashcards.question: What role does your free leg play in escaping the Suloev Stretch?
flashcards.answer: Your free leg is an active escape tool — framing or kicking it through lets you reverse the entanglement into your own control or create the space to clear the trapped leg before the finish locks on.

training_progressions.description: Have a partner slowly enter the leg fold from top half guard while you practice identifying the trap the moment your heel starts toward your buttock, before any compression is applied.
Against light resistance, drill keeping the trapped knee straight and the hip mobile so the partner cannot secure the figure-four, resetting each time you successfully deny the trap.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 3: Hip rotation and foot clearing
training_progressions.description: Add hip rotation away from the compression and hand-fighting to clear the trapped foot, learning to recover top half guard before the partner stacks their weight.
From positional sparring with the trap already partially set, practice kicking the free leg through to reverse the entanglement while tapping early to any genuine compression.
